title: A SOLEMN JUDGMENT AND A NEW HOPE

memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: Then Joshua, together with all Israel, took Achan son of Zerah, the silver, the robe, the gold bar, his sons and daughters, his cattle, donkeys and sheep, his tent and all that he had, to the Valley of Achor. Joshua said, "Why have you brought this trouble on us? The Lord will bring trouble on you today." Then all Israel stoned him, and after they had stoned the rest, they burned them. Over Achan they heaped up a large pile of rocks, which remains to this day. Then the Lord turned from his fierce anger. Therefore that place has been called the Valley of Achor ever since. — Josh 7:24-26 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
This is a heavy passage, and we must not soften its severity. Achan's sin brought a severe judgment, and we should feel its weight. We hold it honestly in its setting: this was a unique moment in Israel's history, under a specific covenant, when the survival and holiness of God's people at the outset of the conquest hung in the balance. The seriousness of the punishment matches the seriousness of what sin does — it brings death and "trouble" (the word Achor means trouble) into the community of God's people.

This account is not a pattern for how we punish wrongdoing today; under the New Covenant, Christ has borne the ultimate penalty for sin. But it does teach us, unforgettably, that sin is deadly serious. We live in an age that treats sin lightly, as harmless or even amusing. Scripture will not let us. Sin costs. It brings trouble. It leads to death (Rom 6:23). We dare not trifle with it.

Yet do not miss the flicker of hope. The place was named the Valley of Achor — the Valley of Trouble. And centuries later, God made an astonishing promise: He would make "the Valley of Achor a door of hope" (Hos 2:15). The very place of judgment would one day become a doorway to hope. That is the gospel written into geography.

For this is what God does in Christ. He takes our valleys of trouble, our places of sin and death, and He makes them doors of hope. At the cross, judgment fell on Jesus so that our trouble might become our gateway to grace. Where sin brought death, Christ brings life. The Valley of Achor becomes a door of hope.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do you take the seriousness of sin as honestly as Scripture does?
2. How does the "Valley of Trouble becoming a door of hope" reveal God's redeeming heart?
3. In what "valley" in your life is God able to open a door of hope through Christ?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Holy God, help me never to treat sin lightly. Thank You that in Christ You turn my valleys of trouble into doors of hope, and that judgment fell on Him so I could live. Amen.
